QF.id: AIFM AIFs in India and Suitability_9

question.text: Mira Family Office has approached Pragati AIF Manager about allocating to a new Category III long-short equity fund. As the AIF Manager, your suitability assessment concludes the family office is an APPROPRIATE LP. Which of the following is the WEAKEST reason to support that conclusion?

answer.text: Family offices typically have high holding capacity and can absorb illiquidity over the fund tenure
Family offices generally have the ability and willingness to take risk commensurate with Cat III's leveraged/derivative strategies
Family offices usually have ticket-size capacity well above the INR 1 crore AIF minimum
Family offices are classified as Retail Investors under SEBI regulations and therefore enjoy enhanced investor protection in Cat III AIFs

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the workbook, AIF capital is privately pooled from select, sophisticated investors rather than the general public. Category III AIFs are described as suitable for institutional investors, family offices, non-resident investors, UHNIs and HNIs, and the AIF minimum investor contribution is INR 1 crore. Family offices are listed among the sophisticated investor categories for whom Cat III is appropriate, not as retail investors with enhanced retail-style protection. The Trap: A is a legitimate suitability factor — family offices typically have high holding capacity and can absorb illiquidity. B is also legitimate — Cat III uses leveraged/derivative strategies and family offices generally have the ability and willingness to take the corresponding risk. C is supported by the INR 1 crore AIF minimum, which family offices comfortably exceed. Only D inverts reality by claiming retail classification and retail-style protection for family offices. Note: AIFs sit outside the retail-protection regime precisely because they target sophisticated investors such as institutions, family offices, UHNIs and HNIs.
